lectures.title: Let ChatGPT Share Its Thought Process (Chain of Thought Prompting)

cues.en: Now, kind of related to the prompting technique explained
in the previous lecture - where we used ChatGPT
to split a problem into multiple sub problems
on our behalf - there is another very powerful
prompting technique you should be aware of.
In certain situations, you can get dramatically better results
by forcing ChatGPT to outline its thought process,
so to say, or, put in other words: If you get ChatGPT to describe
how it derived a certain solution, instead of just giving you the solution,
you can, in certain situations, get way better results.
And the reason for that simply is that in the end, as you learned
in this course ChatGPT, and all these large language
models, are about predicting words in the end.
They are about predicting text based on the text
you passed to them and the text they already generated.
And if they output an entire
thought process that can therefore lead to better results -
since they have more words to build up the overall response
and more words that need to be connected logically -
than if you just ask for a shorter, or single, result, for example.
And here's a pretty good example that shows what I mean.
If you ask ChatGPT for the result of a mathematical calculation -
and you force it to give you just the result without describing
how it got there - chances are that you are getting a wrong result.
For example, here the correct result would have been 80,
but since ChatGPT is no calculator, but instead
just a tool that predicts words, here, it predicted the wrong word.
And of course, as also mentioned before, it's totally possible that you got the
right result for this specific example because there is some randomness involved.
But simply try a couple of different calculations and chances are high
that with this prompt, where you force ChatGPT to give you just one single result
instead of giving you
an entire explanation, you're sometimes getting wrong results.
If you instead would send a prompt that looks something like this,

just give you the final result, but instead kind of derive
the result, chances are that you're getting a correct result.
